#4243. Zelda: Ocarina of Time Review: A Modern Remake With an Old Soul

Nintendo brings one of gaming's most influential adventures into the modern era without losing the magic that made it special.

I don't think I'll ever forget the first time I played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Not because I remember every detail of that first adventure, but because it was literally the first video game I ever played.

I was just a little kid who barely understood English, sitting in front of a Nintendo 64 with a controller (which, yes, wasn't even connected to the console because I was the younger sister) and a dictionary by my side. I had no idea what half the characters were saying, but I knew I wanted to see what happened next. Nearly 30 years later, I find myself returning to that same adventure, this time with a much better understanding of English and a controller that actually works. And, surprisingly enough, I think this might be one of the most emotionally powerful experiences I've had with a remake in a long time.

From Darksiders to Shinobi: Art of Vengeance, I present to you ten action-adventure games that are unexpected masterpieces.

Sure, we all know how revolutionary Ocarina of Time was back in 1998. Its approach to 3D level design, exploration, combat, and storytelling helped shape the entire industry, establishing a reference that countless games would follow for decades. But this remake doesn't seem interested in proving that all over again.

So, rather than trying to reinvent one of gaming's most influential adventures, Nintendo seems much more interested in touching something deeper than any groundbreaking mechanic ever could: the memories we built with this little boy, his fairy, and a world that once felt impossibly big.

For starters, let's get one thing out of the way: despite Nintendo's pre-release marketing describing this as a ground-up remake a few times, don't expect something along the lines of Square Enix's Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy. This is actually a faithful recreation of the original, much closer in spirit to what Nintendo did with Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask on the Nintendo 3DS.

The main story remains practically untouched, the overall structure is familiar, and most of the changes come in the form of visual improvements, quality-of-life adjustments, and a handful of additions that make the experience feel more modern. This means that if you've played the original, you'll recognize almost everything here.

And I can understand that this might disappoint some people. When a remake is announced as being built from the ground up, it's natural to expect substantial changes, perhaps even a new interpretation of familiar locations, mechanics, or story moments. But I think it all comes down to what you expect from this particular adventure in the end.

If you've played the original, you'll recognize almost everything here.

As a longtime Zelda fan who literally learned how to play video games with Link, I found this approach much more effective than I initially imagined, since it allowed the remake to strike a point much deeper than any new fancy level design could ever reach, largely because it understands that Ocarina of Time doesn't need a completely different story to make us feel something all over again.

Instead, it gives us that very same story with a series of carefully considered tweaks. Some are immediately noticeable, while others are the kind of little details you might not even realize have changed until you've spent a few hours exploring Hyrule again. And there's no better place to start discussing these changes than with the story itself.

If you've somehow never experienced Ocarina of Time, here's the short version: you're a little boy without a fairy who happens to oversleep one morning, only to be awakened by a very concerned fairy named Navi. Before long, you're thrown into a journey to save the world, involving a mysterious princess and an evil Gerudo king.

It's a wonderfully straightforward premise that gradually evolves into something much bigger, exploring themes of childhood, growing up, loss, and how the passage of time feels bittersweet for us all. And, nearly three decades later, its emotional impact remains remarkably intact. However, the remake introduces something that makes these familiar moments feel considerably more powerful: dedicated cutscenes with voice acting.

The original Ocarina of Time did an incredible job with the hardware limitations of the Nintendo 64. Seriously, the developers managed to create some wonderfully expressive moments with not much to work with back then. But now, these scenes finally have the cinematic presentation they've always deserved – and boy, does it make a difference!

I honestly lost count of how many times I caught myself wearing the dumbest smile while watching a cutscene. Seeing Princess Ruto slowly abandon her grumpy attitude as she falls for Link, watching Darunia dance to Saria's Song as if he's attending the greatest concert of his life, or witnessing the moment we realize Ganondorf only managed to obtain the power he wanted because we essentially fell for his little scheme.

These scenes have so much more personality now, and the voice performances help give familiar characters a newfound sense of life. More importantly, they made me realize something rather unexpected: deep down, these were already the scenes I had imagined back in 1998. As a child, we had essentially created a full version of these moments in our heads, but the remake gave those childhood interpretations a proper visual and emotional form, and that's a pretty wonderful achievement!

More importantly, they made me realize something rather unexpected: deep down, these were already the scenes I had imagined back in 1998.

And speaking of giving familiar characters more room to breathe, there's another storytelling improvement here that I absolutely love: how NPCs are way more important now.

The remake's dev team included younger folks, several of whom never played the original Ocarina of Time, who provided a much-needed modern view of things.

One of my favorite things about Ocarina of Time has always been its worldbuilding. Hyrule is filled with strange, charming, and occasionally downright questionable people, each with their own little stories and quirks. But the remake takes this aspect of the original and expands it in a surprisingly meaningful way.

Here's a tiny detail that makes a huge difference around here: time now passes continuously within Hyrule's towns. Basically, in the original, the world essentially had four different environmental states: Child Link during the day and night, and Adult Link during the day and night. This allowed certain characters and events to appear depending on the time period and Link's age, but the system was somewhat restrictive because time wouldn't actually progress while you were exploring towns.

Now, the remake changes that! The sun rises and sets naturally as you explore even inside cities, with characters appearing and disappearing according to their own schedules (except in more contained areas such as temples and minigame shops).

It's a small adjustment that makes the towns feel much more organic, almost as if their inhabitants finally have their own agendas, which gives it a lovely Majora’s Mask vibe. Also, this adds additional events and dialogue associated with these new day-night cycles, giving us more opportunities to learn about people we previously knew very little about.

My favorite example of this is Grog, who is arguably one of the saddest characters in the entire game. Remember that punk-looking guy who sits beneath a tree in Kakariko Village at night, complaining that everyone he knows is disgusting? In the original, we only really encounter him twice: once as Child Link and later in the Lost Woods as Adult Link. Well, thanks to the new time system, you can now find him walking around Kakariko Village during the day, too. And he has more dialogue and new interactions, finally giving more weight to fan theories that have circulated about him for nearly 30 years!

And this isn’t an isolated example. Several other characters receive similar attention, making Hyrule feel like a much more interconnected place. I absolutely love this kind of addition because it doesn't just give us more content for the sake of having more content. It actually enriches a world we already know, rewards longtime fans who have spent years discussing its little mysteries, and makes its characters feel like actual inhabitants rather than people waiting for Link to show up. It just makes everything feel a little more real.

Okay, so the remake has the storytelling side covered. But what about the actual gameplay? After all, Ocarina of Time wouldn't have become such an influential title without its approach to exploration, combat, and puzzle-solving.

The good news is that the core experience remains remarkably faithful, although there are plenty of quality-of-life improvements that make returning to Hyrule considerably more comfortable.

For starters, the item menu has been reduced to three main tabs, with a much cleaner organization that makes finding and equipping things considerably easier. I have to admit that I wasn't particularly fond of the menu taking direct inspiration from Breath of the Wild, since different games have very different needs. However, the new quick-access carousel is an absolute lifesaver, and switching between items during exploration and combat feels much more fluid. You no longer have to spend quite so much time navigating menus just to equip something.

And there's also a second quick-access system dedicated to some of your most essential tools, including the Ocarina, Lens of Truth, Happy Mask Salesman's masks, and (yes, you can finally celebrate!) the Iron Boots. This last addition is particularly welcome because it addresses one of the most infamous frustrations of the original game: the Water Temple.

But don't think everything is perfect just because most changes are improvements. Some of the modernized design decisions have introduced a few restrictions that, to be completely honest, I'm not entirely convinced were necessary. For instance, certain pieces of equipment have been tweaked to prevent players from using them in ways the developers seemingly never intended.

This happened with the Hookshot, which was previously a wonderful tool for experimenting with different traversal possibilities, but now only attaches to specific designated surfaces. That means you can no longer use it to reach rooftops, for example. Does this force you to find alternative solutions? Sure. But it also takes away some of the creativity and freedom that made experimenting with the original game's mechanics so much fun.

Still, this is where expectations come into play again. And there is something important to highlight: overall, the remake makes your life considerably easier than it was back in 1998, which means that finding new solutions isn’t actually hard. Around here, NPCs offer more hints and several sequences have been optimized to deliver a more straightforward experience. Oh, and there's also a dedicated quest log that helps you keep track of both the main adventure and your secondary objectives.

While I wasn't particularly happy about the Hookshot changes, I never felt like they significantly compromised my experience. Finding alternative solutions was generally okay, and the improvements elsewhere made the overall gameplay feel much smoother. So it's a trade-off, and one that I think works more often than it doesn't.

Eiji Aonuma and the development team for the Ocarina of Time remake discussed how one of the original's infamous dungeons is being improved.

Now, here's where things get a little more complicated. As you might expect from a remake that's practically a 1:1 recreation, exploration remains very faithful to the original. And while the quality-of-life improvements make moving around Hyrule much more pleasant, they don't necessarily change how you interact with the world itself.

There are some additional visual indicators to help you find interesting things, though. Poes in Hyrule Field are now associated with specific fences, and Lake Hylia is no longer “separated” from the field, for example, making some environmental details easier to identify locations worth investigating. But the overall level design is pretty much what we experienced back in 1998, for better or worse.

And I have mixed feelings about that. On one hand, revisiting these locations with modernized controls and an entirely new visual presentation is an incredibly emotional experience. I genuinely enjoyed wandering around places I hadn't seen in years, recognizing familiar spots, and discovering little details that I had completely forgotten about. It's the kind of experience that makes you want to stop every few minutes just to appreciate how much care went into recreating this world.

On the other hand, I can't help wondering whether the developers could have gone a little further, especially since Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom have completely changed our expectations of what exploring Hyrule can mean, giving us approximately 984,396 things to discover while traveling from point A to point B. Compared to those experiences, Ocarina of Time's more structured approach can feel a little restrictive, particularly when you know exactly where everything is supposed to be.

I would have loved to see a few more surprises along the way, perhaps additional secrets or expanded areas that rewarded players for approaching familiar locations from a different perspective. But, once again, I need to consider what this remake is trying to accomplish. As someone with an almost unhealthy amount of nostalgia running through my veins, I honestly didn't mind revisiting a place I consider home, even if the journey remained largely unchanged! However, if you're expecting a completely redesigned Hyrule with new exploration mechanics and substantially expanded areas, I'd recommend keeping those expectations in check.

Now, let's talk about the elephant in the room: the visuals. The remake retains the colorful, whimsical identity of the original, but practically everything has been reimagined from an aesthetic standpoint. Hyrule now looks even more like a fantasy world, with lush environments, intricate textures, expressive character models, and an almost overwhelming amount of environmental detail.

I have to confess that the new art direction took some getting used to. Kokiri Forest, in particular, initially felt a little too dense for my taste. Come on, don't any of these Kokiri kids own a lawn mower? And Young Link's redesigned appearance also gave me some mixed feelings during my first few hours.

But the more I played, the more the new aesthetic grew on me. Before I knew it, I was completely obsessed with how beautiful everything looked. And a big part of that comes down to the character designs. Rather than simply updating existing models with higher-resolution textures, the developers have reimagined several characters and enemies to better fit the remake's more elaborate fantasy aesthetic. The result feels cohesive, and there's a clear sense of inspiration behind practically every design.

Not to mention the little details! You can see (and feel, since this game is all about feelings, right?) just how much attention went into recreating familiar locations. Kakariko Village's well, for example, now features carefully rendered water and a variety of textures that make the environment feel considerably more tangible. Even something as simple as watching Link play the Ocarina becomes a visual treat, since you can actually see his fingers moving to the correct notes.

Also, the developers clearly know which details longtime fans care about. One particularly memorable example is how they've handled one of the game's most terrifying creatures (you know who!), since it is scarier than ever. And several bosses have also received additional visual details and updated animations that make their encounters feel more imposing.

And it's these little touches that make the difference! The remake doesn't just want Hyrule to look prettier; it wants every familiar corner to feel worth revisiting. And, honestly, I could spend hours just walking around and appreciating it all.

Putting everything together, I think it's fair to say that this is a remake that successfully modernizes a classic without losing its old soul. And considering how heavily nostalgia has influenced the gaming industry lately, with remakes and remasters seemingly arriving every other month, it's nice to see one that understands exactly what made its source material so special.

Most of the improvements are welcome, even if a few decisions (sorry, I still won't forgive what happened to the Hookshot) leave something to be desired. The updated gameplay makes the experience feel much more accessible, the visual overhaul is gradually gorgeous, and the additional storytelling touches give familiar characters a newfound sense of personality.

Putting everything together, I think it's fair to say that this is a remake that successfully modernizes a classic without losing its old soul.

There are also several additions that I’m obsessed with, from hearing iconic characters speak for the first time to seeing long-standing fan theories receive more attention, not to mention the extra Ocarina mechanics that let you hum melodies into the microphone to play them. It's a collection of thoughtful changes that, when put together, makes this adventure feel surprisingly fresh without sacrificing what made it so memorable.

And that's precisely why I think this remake works so well for longtime fans. It doesn't ask us to forget the original or replace the memories we built with it. Instead, it gives us an opportunity to experience those same feelings again, now with a presentation and gameplay that feel right at home in 2026. But I also believe it works wonderfully as an entry point for newcomers! Despite its faithful structure, the modernized controls, expanded guidance, and quality-of-life improvements make the experience feel far less dated than the original. So you can still appreciate everything that made Ocarina of Time revolutionary without having to deal with every limitation of a game released nearly three decades ago.

In the end, this remake made me feel like that little kid again, waking up early on Saturday mornings to spend hours exploring Hyrule, controller in hand (and, thankfully, connected this time). And I could feel that this was exactly what Nintendo wanted to accomplish within the first few minutes.

Playing this remake reminded me that video games can be much more than the mechanics we praise, the level design we analyze, the technical achievements we celebrate, or framerates that we fear to drop. Sometimes, their greatest power lies in how they make us feel, even decades after we've first experienced them – and Ocarina of Time still has that magic. Now, if you'll excuse me, I still have a few Golden Skulltulas and Heart Pieces to collect. And then? Well, I think I'm ready for another adventure.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the most beloved games of all time, but these remakes might be just as meaningful to fans.

#4238. The Sims 4 developer hasn't forgotten about its quality of life commitment, and is back with an update on what to expect in 2026

Maxis has offered some fresh details on its long-running mission to improve player quality of life in The Sims 4.

As the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of new content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

The quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one update on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

In the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of issues should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

The first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

The infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo issues, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Another important area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

The good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next update will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported issues.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.

#4236. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Goes Nuclear Against ‘Lobby Shopping’

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Players have used third-party applications to assist their play for years now, to mixed success and intent. Many benign apps for games like League and Valorant give easier access to community info, while other, more malicious cheats can completely ruin a game for everyone else in the lobby.

After unjustly banning a Battlefield 6 player, EA lost a court case to keep the ban in place.

Call of Duty: Warzone players have been utilizing one of the oddest forms of cheating I’ve ever heard of, peeking at the skill level of everyone in the lobby through the app Warzone Agent to decide whether or not to just leave the game. Activision has announced they’re clamping down hard on the practice, looking to eliminate it going forward.

Call of Duty players have been complaining about the franchise’s skill-based matchmaking (SBMM) for years now, a system where players are matched against foes equivalent to their skill level. This is, of course, how most matchmaking systems work, but COD players have been asking for its elimination since the original Modern Warfare remake.

In order to avoid these close matches, they utilize apps like Warzone Agent to figure out the average rank of the lobby before deciding to play, a practice Warzone’s anti-cheat division, Ricochet, has officially stood against. In their release surrounding the practice of lobby shopping, “moving forward, players who leave Warzone Agent loaded will not be able to access Multiplayer modes.”

Lobby shopping is the practice of hopping around warm-up stage lobbies to search for one with a lower skill ceiling, essentially targeting worse players to maximize your own boons. Activision has made it clear they won’t stand to suffer the practice any longer, further saying, “using unauthorized software to manipulate the player experience violates Activision Terms of Use and leaves your account and hardware subject to enforcement.”

Many benign apps for games like League and Valorant give easier access to community info, while other, more malicious cheats can completely ruin a game for everyone else in the lobby.

Threatening to drop the ban hammer on violators is a great way to shake the practice off, and Activision isn’t stopping there, clarifying what it considers cheating. That includes external account boosting, led by swarms of bots they’ve managed to start stomping out.

Bots plague any free-to-play game people want to put time into, and focusing more on curtailing them is a great step toward slowing the flow, even if it is just a bandage over the wound. For now, Activision has drawn their line in the sand. The only question is whether or not they’ll flinch in the face of community complaints, but they’ve stuck by their guns this long.

The community complaint around skill-based matchmaking has always struck me as incredibly odd, with these players mostly desiring a true random selection process. These random matches are, on paper, more varied, but in practice lead to matches that are total stomps for one side or the other, leaving plenty of players with a bad taste in their mouths.

Getting to be the one stomping can be great fun, but that’s also possible against players of your skill level. SBMM’s main purpose is to minimize the games that feel like complete wipes from the loser’s perspective, keeping them playing against those who are actually equivalent to them on a broad scale. It’s far from perfect, but it's better than literally just tossing a random selection of players in a room.

Without it, not only would many casual players have to gamble on getting crushed every other game, but Activision could lose those players after enough rough matches, the true reason for the practice’s continued support. Despite the complaints, Activision has clearly long since decided that skill-based matchmaking is the best middle ground for skilled and casual players alike, giving everyone designated lobbies where they’re at least promised matches that are competitive.

Modern Warfare 4's launch party is still going, with a free play period for DMZ ready to rake in new players.

#4235. Genshin Impact fans on PS4 only have six weeks to find another platform as support winds down with one final update

Premium in-game purchases have now been disabled on PlayStation 4, as one of Genshin's four original launch platforms prepares to get dropped in early April.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

HoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's update.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

These have included roles such as SEO Editor, Managing Editor at DualShockers, and Global Head of Gaming, and he's also been seen on the BBC. He’s also interviewed some of the world’s biggest musical artists to find out how the medium has inspired their work, and TV and Film actors about their roles in video game adaptations. Alongside this, Sam focuses on breaking news. While Phantom Blade Zero is a truly excellent game (scoring a 5/5 in my official review), players have been hard at work doing what they can to improve it in the 10 days since it launched. We've seen full Soulslike transformations, game-changing cheat menus, and the addition of Sun Wukong from Chinese folklore.

It feels like the type of game that's going to get consistent support from its already ginormous player base, with that support continuing over recent times. One player is seemingly on a mission to make the game's best bosses into playable characters, with three already completed and ready to go.

Over on Nexus Mods, creator QOutlaw has been creating playable versions of some of Phantom Blade Zero's most memorable bosses. They've made three so far, and they're all excellent.

The first they released was a playable version of Bai Chilian, including her outfits and voice. It's received over 23,000 downloads so far.

Bai Chilian is arguably the best boss from Phantom Blade Zero's second area, Crimson Forest. She has two phases: the first is a more grounded fight where she summons ribbon snakes to aid her in battle. In the second, she becomes possessed, attacking from strings around the arena. If you collect all of the memory flowers related to her, you are assisted in battle by one of Soul's allies. It's a great fight, and while you'll be playing as her base form in this mod, equipping the White Serpent and Crimson Viper swords will make it a lot of fun.

The second mod QOutlaw uploaded is a playable Yuding- No.12 Crescent Blade Puppet. This fight happens late in Phantom Blade Zero and has some of the best animations in the entire game. She also blesses you with what I believe is the best weapon of the game's 30. Probably not as iconic as Bai Chilian, but a great option.

The final mod turns Soul into Mo Yuan, the masked man found in the Loong challenges, played by Donnie Yen. He's a pivotal character in Phantom Blade Zero's overarching story and is vital to the game's true ending. He's also exceptionally cool. And he's Donnie Yen.

I love the work that modders do, and installing any of these will make future NG+ runs of Phantom Blade Zero feel entirely different. A big recommendation from me.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

#4225. Killing Floor 3 Studio Announces Layoffs After Publishing Hire Spree

Lauren has experience in the gaming and esports space, writing news, guides, features, reviews, lists, conducting interviews, and more. Before joining the team at DualShockers, Lauren was a Features Writer at Adventure Gamers, a Guides Writer at Gameranx, as well as contributing as a News Writer at PCInvasion and Daily

Layoffs are always devastating for the video game industry and the people affected. Unfortunately, they have become all too common, and whether it’s a small studio or a large household name, it seems nobody is safe in today’s climate.

Tripwire Interactive, best known for the Killing Floor series, is the latest studio to be hit by layoffs. The studio was founded back in 2005, and Embracer Group acquired Tripwire Interactive through its former subsidiary, Saber Interactive, in 2022.

In our Killing Floor 3 Review, we go over what could have worked and what didn't in the end for Tripwire's latest game.

In a statement published on the official Tripwire Interactive X account, the studio says it “has undergone a workforce reduction, affecting 36 talented people across our studio. This was certainly not an easy decision, but unfortunately, a necessary one for the organization.”

Tripwire Interactive describes the impacted employees as “truly great people who are exceptional at their roles,” and vows to “help and support these individuals with compassion and dignity during transition.”

The team will continue to focus on Maneater 2, which was officially announced as part of Sony’s September State of Play. It’s expected to launch sometime in 2027.

As the name suggests, Maneater 2 is the sequel to 2021’s Maneater, an action-packed RPG where you are the biggest threat in the open-world oceans that you’ll traverse. There are new evolutions, discoveries to be made, and a whole lot of opportunities to become the villain.

It has also been confirmed that work will continue on Killing Floor 3, as the developers try to salvage the rocky start the game had when it was released back in July 2025. Killing Floor 3 reviews remain mixed among critics and players, and updates are still rolling out, containing new content and fixes.

This isn’t the first time this year that Tripwire Interactive has held layoffs. On March 4, the studio cut its workforce by 23 people, meaning this new round of layoffs brings Tripwire Interactive’s total this year to 59. Only time will tell if any of Tripwire Interactive’s projects will suffer from delays as a result of these layoffs.

Similar to this instance, a real reason wasn’t provided for the March 4 layoffs, instead citing: “As the gaming industry continues to evolve, so do the needs of our studios, which means understanding our long-term strategy and aligning with business realities where needed in order to stay focused on our key creative goals.”

Tripwire Interactive describes the impacted employees as “truly great people who are exceptional at their roles,” and vows to “help and support these individuals with compassion and dignity during transition.”

On November 4, 2026, Tripwire Presents, the publishing sector of Tripwire Interactive, announced that it would be expanding its business to include scaled publishing support for indie developers to help put the spotlight on indie titles from across a variety of genres. The purpose of the initiative is to provide greater visibility for self-published indie games that Tripwire believes fans will enjoy.

It has been confirmed that Tripwire Presents will continue to go ahead with their plans, and the games that have already been chosen are The Boss Gangster: Criminal Empire, Starforged Legacy, Mars Attracts, One-Eyed Likho, and Eslabong.

This round of redundancies adds another to the tally of alarmingly large video game industry layoffs just this year alone. Other examples include Sucker Punch making staff cuts shortly after the launch of the Complete Edition of Ghost of Yōtei, and, of course, the mass layoffs conducted by XBOX.

Another three rounds of XBOX layoffs are slated to begin this month and last into the new year.

While The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Switch 2 remake is a faithful (and truly excellent) reimagining of what many consider to be the greatest game ever created, Nintendo did make some big concessions.

It further censored a scene featuring Ganondorf, where his previously red blood, which had later been turned green, was removed, and it also replaced paintings of Mario found in Hyrule Castle so as not to "interrupt" immersion. However, while it did remove one big Nintendo reference, one fan is convinced the company added another, pointing to a cloud they believe looks like Kirby.

Over on Reddit, a new post has appeared on the Nintendo Switch 2 subreddit, and it's proven highly controversial. The original poster, Faded_Link, claimed to have found a Kirby Easter egg: a cloud floating over Hyrule. The cloud in question is round and looks like it has two little arms and feet, just like Kirby. I very much see the correlation.

It seems, though, like I am one of the few, and the post in question has drawn a lot of heat. Despite almost 7,000 upvotes, many of the 500 comments have spoken out against the validity of the Kirby cloud.

Many opted to post gifs of people squinting, or implied the original poster was perhaps on some hard substances, and the implication was that Nintendo wouldn't remove Mario just to add Kirby. However, Kirby is canon in the Zelda universe...

Anti-Kirby is an enemy found in Link's Awakening and its remake, and is a horrifying version of the beloved pink blob with a disconcerting smile and a slightly off-brand color.

There was some support for the original poster, with one commenter saying, "Idk why you're getting ribbed for this, I saw it immediately. Good eye," but the overwhelming consensus was negative.

I'm not sure how that's the case, though. If you look at our beautiful artistic rendition of the cloud featuring Kirby above, it's clear as day. Or maybe I'm just losing my mind...

#4220. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 is about to launch a couple of major initiatives that may not exactly be what players have been looking for.

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

The Warlock is one of two classes coming to Diablo 4 with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion. The first, the Paladin, is already available in the game for anyone who pre-orders the expansion. The Warlock will instead arrive alongside the expansion on April 28.

The Developer Update will also include a first look at the game’s next season (Season 12), currently set for March 10. This mini season will only last until the expansion’s release, so it’s going to be interesting to see what it brings to the game.

You’ll be able to watch the showcase live at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT on Diablo 4’s official YouTube, Twitch, and Twitter channels. We’ve embedded the YouTube and Twitch players below for your convenience.

Among the topics the Developer Update will cover are the Killstreaks system, as well as Bloodstained items. As always, you can also expect a Q&A segment at the end of the show, and I imagine there’s going to be a few about the Warlock.

#4215. Diablo 4's next season is short, but it lets you become The Butcher, and it has Doom: The Dark Ages skins you probably can't afford

Blizzard has unveiled the next Diablo 4 season, which kicks off next week to hold us over until the launch of the game's big expansion in April.

The big Diablo 4 Developer Update has indeed delivered the goods. One of the livestream’s big topics was, of course, the game’s upcoming mini-season, which is set to kick off next week and run until the launch of Lord of Hatred, the game’s anticipated next expansion.

You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.

Season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion. Many of the season’s biggest additions were available to preview in the 2.6.0 Public Test Realm.

Patch 2.6.0, as you might have guessed, is the one that will kick off the slaughter next week. The headline feature here is ability to become The Butcher, the iconic in-game boss who randomly invades players’ games.

When you play as The Butcher, you’ll be rewarded the more kills you get in quick succession. Your skills hotbar will transform to become something more fitting of The Butcher, making them more brutal. You’ll also earn a seasonal currency as you play.

Starting the seasonal questline is how you can begin to assume The Butcher’s form. A Taste of Power can be initiated from Gea Kul. Transforming into The Butcher can be done in a few ways. As you play, you’ll earn Meaty Offerings, which can later be spent on Shrines of Slaughter in the new Helltide. Once activated, the shrine will draw more enemies towards you.

If you never venture into PvP zones in Diablo 4, this season may change your mind. The standard PvP combat that could only be found in Fields of Hatred has been replaced with a Ceremony of Slaughter, a new event that rewards you for killing enemies quickly. See it through and The Butcher’s Idol will spawn, allowing you to transform into it.

Elsewhere in the world, you’ll also be able to attain the same power at Slaughterhouses, a new activity type available this season. Inside, you immediately become The Butcher for the entirety of the run.

The Butcher’s arrival also ties into two of the other Season of Slaughter’s more interesting additions. First, the Killstreak system finally arrives in Diablo 4, rewarding you for being as efficient as possible in carving your way through enemies.

Anyone who played Diablo 3 should be familiar with how it works. It kicks off the moment you get a kill, and has a visible timer where you’ll need continue performing the same action to up your streak. The more kills you get, the more often your timer will refresh.

There are five tiers to climb through: Killstreak, Carnage, Devastation, Bloodbath, and Massacre. You’re awarded for the tier you manage to reach before the timer runs out. You’ll earn XP and seasonal rep each time a Killstreak is achieved.

The other Butcher-themed addition is Bloodied Items, which is a new item quality available throughout this season. They play into the Killstreak system to grant you even more power. Bloodied Items come with unique affixes that scale off your Killstreak tier. You’ll see many familiar items in that pool, as any item in the game has a chance to drop as Bloodied. Bloodied Items can also be acquired by earning Fresh Meat.

Even if none of that sounds exciting, you’re probably going to redownload the game for The Paladin free trial, which kicks off alongside the new season on March 11. The trial is only available until March 18, and it lets you try out the Paladin class.

The trial is available across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. You’ll be able to take the new class for a spin, but your progress will be capped at level 25. The Paladin can be permanently unlocked by buying the Lord of Hatred expansion, as it’s one of two classes the expansion is introducing.

The good news is that any progress you make in the free trial will carry over to the full game if/when you buy the expansion.

Season of Slaughter also kicks off a Doom: The Dark Ages collaboration event. As we’ve come to expect, there’s a very limited free component to the collaboration, in the form of the Doom Reliquary. This is essentially a mini-battle pass that includes the Shield Saw skin, Slayer’s Flair, the head of the Cyberdemon as a back trophy and various other smaller bits.

The more impressive items - such as character skins, will instead be available to purchase for real money. The list includes the Doom Slayer armor, Mecha Dragon Serrat skin for your cat mount, and a Cacodemon pet.

Though the armor skin is cross-class compatible, judging by how much previous collaboration items have cost in Diablo 4, most of us probably won’t be spending that kind of money to get it.

#4214. "Creation without a creator": Pathologic 3's devs have refused to patch an invisible apple tree, and for a blissful moment, I thought they were lying to poison Google's AI

"Maybe this apple tree is trying to tell us something."

Magnificent, depressing plague colony fable Pathologic 3 has received a sizeable game update that adds some new difficulty modes, a photo feature, and some new, worryingly folkloric methods of defeating a murky embodiment of disease. Developers Ice Pick Lodge have also staunchly refused to remove an invisible apple tree, describing this apparently "famous" bug as a hallmark of a game whose "symbolic nature has almost overtaken its function as a product". This appears to be the last major update for Pathologic 3, so that invisible apple tree is staying in the game forever.

I confess, when I first read the Steam blog in question, I doubted. The thing about invisible apple trees is that they are quite easy to confuse with apple trees that are simply not there. Pathologic in general is a house of lies: as Quintin Smith (RPS in peace) put it in his legendary Butchering Pathologic trilogy, "absolutely everybody has an angle, everyone's bending the truth and trying to twist you round their fingers." Pathologic 3 especially is a purgatorial time travel story that must be continually rewritten, a crock of festering rumours enclosed by an enormous, phantom theatre. As such, I read Ice-Pick's typically professorial account of the "invisible apple tree" with intense suspicion.

"Roger Ebert, the famous film critic, once argued that video games could never be art," the devs write on Steam. "It's curious, then, that urinals and bottle racks achieved that status with hardly any struggle, thanks to Marcel Duchamp. So Myst, StarCraft, or Pathologic can't be art, but a urinal can? The distinction, perhaps, lies in function. A urinal placed in a museum stops being plumbing and becomes a symbol. A video game, on the other hand, remains a functional object. We still have to use it.

"But enough about urinals," they go on. "Let's turn to another famous work: Joseph Kosuth's One and Three Chairs. In this work, a chair is no longer simply something to sit on. Whether it's comfortable hardly matters: as a work of art, it still functions. A video game can also become a symbolic chair. But you still have to sit on it. There's a running joke that Pathologic is a great game that nobody actually plays. Somehow, it really has become something like Kosuth's symbolic chair, one nobody is obliged to sit on. Which raises a question: should we even fix Pathologic if its symbolic nature has almost overtaken its function as a product?

"Take visual bugs, for instance. Are they broken chairs you can't sit on, or artistic decisions?" Ice-Pick continue. "Consider our famous invisible apple tree. Oh, apple tree! Why are you here? What are we supposed to do with you? This is probably the most famous bug in Pathologic 3. We've received more complaints about it than almost anything else. We have to admit there were moments when we genuinely hated that tree. Are we going to fix it in this update? Perhaps not.

"After all, it's a creation of the machine," they conclude. "Somehow, the game's code produced this impossible object. And over time, our annoyance at it has begun to turn into a strange affection. Sometimes an artistic act lies not in creating something, but in the artist's decision about it. Maybe this apple tree is trying to tell us something. So the tree stays."

Aside from making me pine for a world in which, say, EA add a "hypernormalisation" slider to The Sims, or Ubisoft redefine Assassin's Creed parkour as a Situationist dérive (yes, I too have read books), the blog post filled me with confusion. I couldn't remember any invisible apple trees in Pathologic 3. I also couldn't find any English language mention of Pathologic 3's avowedly "famous" ethereal vegetation on Google or the Steam forums, save for in stories covering the game's latest update.

My weakness for talk of symbolism notwithstanding, I began to worry that Ice-Pick might be winding us up. And by "us", I specifically mean pathetic videogame reporters, hunting for a cool bug anecdote to wrap a headline around. Pathetic videogame reporters who are subject to the wiles of Google Search, which has recently become an AI-driven abomination that subsumes and rewords all knowledge while starving actual information sources of traffic.

There have been efforts to screw with Google's AI summaries, planting nonsense on Reddit and elsewhere in the hope of skewing or outright sabotaging the chatbot's datasets. Perhaps Pathologic 3's "invisible apple tree" was one such poison apple, I mused to myself, offered to Gemini in the manner of a cackling forest hag thrusting suspiciously plump and juicy fruit at cherubic village children. Associations foamed in my brain: Ice-Pick Lodge are based in Kazakhstan... where apples first grew in the wild. Breathless, I contacted Ice-Pick Lodge for a clarification, and – bah, it turns out there is an invisible apple tree in Pathologic 3, after all.

"The slightly longer story goes like this," producer Alexander Souslov told me over DM. "At some point (nobody remembers exactly when), one of our tree assets - an apple tree, to be precise - started rendering incorrectly and became invisible. The leaves were still there, but the trunk was gone. We tried to fix it, but ran into the classic game developer's dilemma: is this really important enough to spend resources on, rather than, say, making another cutscene or putting together another quest?"

Souslov says the apple tree drove him "absolutely nuts". (I feel like he could have rolled with some line about "one bad apple spoiling the barrel", but hey, I'm not one of those stuffed shirts over at Edge Magazine - I don't mind interviewees mixing their arboreal metaphors.) Eventually, however, he made peace with the exasperatingly trunkless tree. "I started thinking: wait a minute, this thing basically came into existence all by itself. Do I really have to fix it?

"And that's when I remembered Marcel Duchamp and his ideas, and suddenly I began to feel that we'd accidentally created something beautiful," Souslov went on. "Invisible trees next to the Cathedral, where time flows in different directions. There's a strange kind of beauty in that, in the very act of creation without a creator.

"So I made an executive artistic decision: we're keeping the tree, and we're officially declaring it part of the world. So no pranks involved! Just a happy accident elevated to the status of artistic intent."

With Souslov's guidance, I fired up an old Pathologic 3 save and tracked down the invisible apple tree in-game, right next to the aforesaid Cathedral. Please find a picture of the thing's spectral foliage below – poetically captured by moonlight at the dead of 1am, through a fog of in-game Apathy. I also belatedly checked Reddit, and yep, there's a paper trail, though Souslov added that the bug is inconsistent: "their whimsical behavior makes it even better as an artistic expression - the apple tree may decide it won't meet with you today."

I remain compelled by the idea of developers telling dirty great porkies in their patchnotes, if only to excite and upset games journalists who really don't have this much time to spare. Mojang used to do that thing with Herobrine, remember?

Given the escalating chatbotification of everything, I think we are entering an exhilarating new age of lying on the internet, in which deceit and doublespeak have become weapons of resistance against the algorithm. But I also just think videogames and their creators are often more fun when they are two-faced, providing there's some fundamental benevolence involved. Videogames are all about sleight of hand, and devs should take more pleasure in that. Thank you to Pathologic 3 for planting this seed.

#4213. LGS Owners Continue To Debate Universes Beyond MTG Sets With Prerelease Figures

Despite Magic: The Gathering's creator, Wizards of the Coast, insistingthat Universes Beyond is largely a well-supported and popular part of the game, it's getting hard to ignore the persistent negative narrative around these sets when prerelease comes around.

Star Trek officially hit prerelease last Friday, and while I enjoyed my own experience at my LGS, it's impossible to ignore the waves of disparaging comments online, whether it be about attendance, playability, or the fact that stores are reportedly being forced to buy Universes Beyond stock under threat of having in-universe stock limited if they don't.

Early online responses to the set and prerelease are bleak, and when you combine that with complaints from players who were willing to buy and invest in the set but couldn't get stock in some cases, it paints a picture of a poor end to 2026. The key, however, is that the negative voices are vocal online players and represent a minority of the game's audience, and this is becoming a consistent trend after the release of Universes Beyond sets that don't fit the typical Venn diagram of Magic players' presumed interests, because the silence after the release of The Hobbit was deafening.

The post that prompted my deeper look at how the Star Trek prerelease was performing overall came from Robert Taylor, in response to a call from Saffron Olive asking how the events were shaping up. The post, which is still live on Twitter / X, has Robert sharing attendance numbers for all of this year's pre-release events at their local store, Mayhem Comics in Iowa.

As you can see from the tweet above, Star Trek had the worst attendance of any event held at that store this year, with 62 attendees, while all in-universe sets had figures above 110. This is, of course, meaningless. It's one store's figure with zero context, but it's useful data when combined with the huge wave of other figures shared across social media and Reddit.

Players are reporting that Star Trek was the outright worst, or among the worst attended events of the year, with the common phrase I'm seeing in posts being "around half" when comparing Star Trek to Reality Fracture, Secrets of Strixhaven, and even The Hobbit.

Personally, my LGS has a capacity of 60, spread across two days: 40 on Friday and 20 on Saturday, while Marvel Super Heroes, Reality Fracture, and The Hobbit were sell-outs; Star Trek wasn't, but it wasn't poorly attended either. Four spaces remained for Friday and four for Saturday, so given the time of year and proximity to other sets, this isn't a bad result.

On the belief that store owners are being forced to overstock Universes Beyond products under threat that they will not receive any in-universe stock as a repercussion, the two WPN store owners who I spoke to deny this, with one going so far as to say they felt safe ordering less Star Trek stock based on customer interest and have been given no indications that their Nauctis stock is suffering as a result.

If you're getting ready to head to your LGS for Star Trek prerelease, then here's everything you need to know about the latest Universes Beyond set.

Wizards of the Coast won't reveal any stats or figures from the prerelease or launch of Star Trek unless they are positive, meaning we'll need to wait until the new year and the next financial update to find out what impact the set had, positive or negative, on sales figures.

Despite all the online bickering, a number of players and store owners believe they have identified the biggest reason Star Trek numbers are down in their areas: Reality Fracture was only six weeks ago.

Granted, there's an entire payday between the two sets, but given the current state of the world and Magic, players may have had to choose between the two sets and decided to put the larger chunk of their cash and time into the in-universe set.

We now have just over two months until the Nauctis: The Sunken Realm prerelease at the end of January, so players have the chance to rest and refresh, ready for a whole new year of Magic. With six sets confirmed on the MTG 2027 calendar, all of which are full-sized and launching with at least four Commander precons, let's just hope that production delays are something we leave behind in 2026, because that's certainly not helping how players are perceiving new sets either.

#4212. Diablo 4’s Warlock looks like an unhinged Necromancer with Sorcerer energy in first look at gameplay

Diablo 4's practitioner of forbidden arts, The Warlock, has been officially unveiled as the second class coming with Lord of Hatred.

Thanks to a meaty, well-produced Diablo 4 Developer Update, we got to have our promised first look at gameplay of the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The showcase offered a deep look at the Warlock’s core archetypes, its gameplay and skills loop, and where the class sits within the game’s existing roster of diverse classes.

Since the initial reveal of Lord of Hatred, The Warlock has remained the mysterious second class. Anyone who pre-purchased the expansion was able to get immediate access to The Paladin, the other class arriving with the expansion. It wasn’t until February that Blizzard officially revealed the class to the world, but we had to wait until this most recent Developer Update to actually see it in action.

The Warlock’s pragmatism exists as the counterpart to The Paladin's purity, in that Warlocks don’t shy away from harnessing the powers of Hell to eliminate their enemies. The class can conjure up demons to do their bidding, and utilise attacks previously only available to legions of Hell.

The Warlock is a hybrid pet and caster class. Their gameplay revolves around summoning demons, and undermining enemies with shadow arts. They rely on two resources: Wrath, and Dominance. Casting Skills consumes Wrath, whereas Dominance is what allows the Warlock to summon and exploit demons.

The Warlock has four archetypes players can spec into. Legions are traditional summoners who rely on overwhelming numbers to crush enemies. Vanguards are closer to Sorcerers, capable of dealing damage head-on. Masterminds utilise shadowcraft to slowly drain their enemies. Finally, Ritualists are summoners of the most terrifying Hell demons.

The Warlock is able to do this by fusing Soul Shards into their bodies. Going down any of the four paths becomes available after reaching level 30, which is when the class mechanic is unlocked. Each Soul Shard is tied to a certain demon, and its through that power that the Warlock is able to call upon them in combat. Your choice does, of course, affect your abilities going forward.

Warlocks arrive alongside new Uniques that cater to their specific playstyles, which is similar to what we’ve previously seen with The Paladin, and The Spiritborn before that.

Lord of Hatred arrives April 28. While we wait, Diablo 4’s next season is kicking off next week to deliver a bit of mindless fun to hold us over until the big day.

#4211. "We basically rewrote the entire State of Decay game": Undead Labs spent years trying to make State of Decay 3 into a full-blown zombie apocalypse MMO

State of Decay 3 was announced with a snazzy cinematic trailer all the way back in 2020. The open-world zombie game was due to move to colder climes, where you would face undead deer and survive the frigid elements. We've since learned that the teaser bore very little resemblance to what was actually being worked on, and was pushed out the door to plump up a Microsoft showcase.

However, what the teaser also didn't reveal was that Undead Labs' ideas for the game were much larger in scope than the two survival games that came before. For several years they were trying to make State of Decay 3 into an MMO that captured the scale of a global zombie apocalypse.

In an interview with GamesIndustry.biz detailing the recent move to independence after Xbox cut the studio loose, Undead Labs CEO Philip Holt explains that the team's founder, Jeff Strain, planned to expand the series from its co-op roots into a full MMO. While Strain left the studio in 2019, his ideas remained with the small team working on the prototypes for State of Decay 3. "He always had a vision of making an MMO and the ultimate global scale of a zombie apocalypse," Holt says. "And so there was just a different set of creative objectives the team was trying to pursue at that time."

After State of Decay 3 was announced in 2020, a small team worked on developing the technology to support an MMO, while the rest of the studio continued supporting State of Decay 2. However, towards the end of 2022, Holt and the team decided to go back to a game that better resembled the scale of the first two games. "There was a pretty significant pivot creatively on State of Decay 3's development," Holt tells GI. "So I would say the game that's present today has really been built probably since '23, maybe late '22." Later in the interview saying "One of the things I learned is just how much respect I have for teams that make successful MMOs, because I've seen them swallow people whole."

It wasn't a flippant change, as it meant throwing out much of what had already been made. "We basically rewrote the entire State of Decay game, and we will not do that again," Holt says. "We have the benefit now of this pretty significant investment in software that we got to figure out how to make the most of. We hope that State of Decay 3 has a long and successful life and becomes a live and evolving game. But yeah, I think it's highly unlikely that we spend as much time on the next game as we did on State of Decay 3."

Though, it did mean that when Xbox cut ties with Undead Labs they had a project near enough to release that they've been able to find a publisher willing to fund State of Decay 3's final months of development. Still, even with that support, Undead Labs still had to lay off "a significant number" of staff.

I've a real soft spot for the state of Decay games, though I've never played them in multiplayer. For me, they were always an apocalypse I could mooch around in solo, gradually expanding my survivors' camp and making a dent in the zombie hordes that roamed across the environment. An MMO take on the same world wouldn't have appealed to my misanthropic sensibilities, but I'm interested to learn how the tech that was produced has been rolled into the current version of State of Decay 3.

Still, one day, I want to face down a zombie deer. Granted, I'll immediately run and hide, but it'd be nice to see one.

So the full game is now titled The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel, or, as we will undoubtedly refer to it moving forward, as we colloquially do with the previous three games (Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim), Sentinel.

The name continues the tradition of naming the games after locations in the Elder Scrolls universe. Oblivion is the sort of exception, as it is a realm, but it still counts. #4209. Hot Wax sets fire to the Tetris playbook with slow-burn puzzle mechanics and a dollop of eldritch menace

Over the past couple of weeks, I've been conscious of an eerie background humming and hissing. For a while I thought it was just tinnitus, brought on by one too many listens of Control's Ashtray Maze OST, but then I realised that it was actually RPS regular quasiotter whispering in my ear about Hot Wax, which launches on Steam this week after a spell of Itch.io exclusivity.

It's the new arcade puzzler from PUNKCAKE Délicieux, otherwise known for inflicting shotguns on chess and forcing the alphabet to wear trousers in the name of archaeology, somehow. Hot Wax is actually quite straightforward by PUNKCAKE standards. It's Tetris, but all the blocks are candles, and rather than filling a line on the grid to clear blocks, you have to plant unpredictably dropped flames on wicks to slowly sizzle the mass away. Relatively straightforward, yes, but fiddly in practice. Did I mention that you're doing all this in a temple, under the eye of a "not unfriendly" eldritch god?

There's still a demo for Hot Wax on Steam, with the full release due in Valve's cathedral of commerce tomorrow. I've had a go at that demo, and it has tickled my brain. You need to line up candles, wick to wick, rather than just filling gaps, as in Tetris. But you still, ideally, need to avoid gaps to slow down the filling of the screen. Once a wick is lit, it'll gradually melt the candle and leap to any other wicks it touches.

Once a candle is lit, you have to avoid smothering it by unscientifically dunking another candle on top of it, while trying to take advantage of how the melting wax alters the layout. I found this enjoyably challenging. And then there are the power-up items, acquired by sacrificing flames to the aforesaid "not unfriendly" god. These include bombs that light a bunch of wicks at once, and acorns that sprout a column-filling sapling. Not sure what they worship in this temple, exactly, other than Tetris.

There will be a bunch of modes in the full release – from basic score attack and endless play, to a mode where you have to melt several, painstakingly arranged candles with just one flame. They're also planning daily seeded challenge runs. As with PUNKCAKE stuff at large, it's a looker, with some lustrous pixel art and lots of nifty little animations. Thank you, quasiotter – this was fun! You can stop going "EEEEEEEE" in my ear now.

#4208. Marathon launch player numbers are about half those of the Server Slam, at least on PC

Marathon hasn't quite been able to attract the same volume of players the recent Server Slam did.

After a couple of delays, a plagiarism lawsuit, and at least one internal reboot, Bungie’s next big game has officially launched. Marathon, the extraction shooter from the studio behind Destiny, has managed to find a decent, if a little small of an audience.

The game’s player numbers on Steam are being compared to its recent free, open weekend, and not in a favourable manner.

Prior to Marathon’s launch, Bungie held a multi-day Server Slam, which offered anyone interested in playing the game a chance to try out almost all of its classes, two of its maps, as well as many of its gameplay and progression systems.

The open test was largely well-received, and players actually showed up for it. It peaked at a very respectable 143,621 concurrent players on Steam, which put it within striking distance of the peak concurrent of its chief competitor, Arc Raiders - at least when you compare both of their pre-launch Server Slam events.

In Arc Raiders’ case, those figures were far outpaced at the game’s actual launch, and the Embark shooter continues to command a very active player base to this day. A paid product garnering far more players than the same product’s own free sampler is never not a good sign, so many hoped something similar would happen with Marathon.

Marathon has now officially launched, and it doesn’t look like it managed to pull an Arc Raiders - at least so far. At its peak, the Bungie shooter attracted 88,337 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), which is a little over half of its Server Slam’s 143,621 peak concurrent.

Numbers have, of course, dropped since then, which is normal, as players log off for the night. This is obviously not the end of the road for Marathon. Friday, and the weekend, may well push numbers closer to the Server Slam heights.

Indeed, word of mouth is quite positive, with the game currently sitting at a Very Positive user review rating on Steam, based on over 4,600 reviews. As has been proven time and time again in recent years, nothing catapults a game like players emphatically advocating for it to their friends, so it could simply be that mainstream players are cautious.

It will become clear where things settle over the weekend.

#4205. Subnautica 2 dev thinks early access teams should worry less about adding features that are "very ugly, incomplete, or prototype"

But acknowledges that "early access" ain't what it was

Subnautica 2 creative director Anthony Gallegos has spoken about what Unknown Worlds have learned over their many years working in Steam early access, exhorting other devs to add new features "as soon as possible" and experiment with them right under the flared nostrils of players. Damn the torpedoes, etcetera.

The original Subnautica is one of the oldest Steam early access success stories, launching in 2014 a month or so after the program went live. Many of the final version's better qualities, including the pivot to horror epitomised by the spectacle of a Reaper grabbing your submarine's face, reflect observation of players and streamers in the wilds.

"Subnautica often launched features when they were very ugly, incomplete, or prototype," Gallegos commented, as part of a group chat about early access with GamesIndustry.biz. "This gave fans a real sense of getting to see game development in progress, in a way few other studios would try, especially for a franchise as big as this."

Unknown Worlds have "cultivated a very empathetic audience through radical transparency," Gallegos continued. "We trust the audience to give us a little grace as we figure things out, and they in turn trust us to make it great in the fullness of time."

Naturally, Gallegos thinks it's vital to keep talking to players and taking their feedback on the chin. "Be honest with them and make them understand how crucial they are to the process," he went on. "Preserve your vision, but listen to them and let them help you bring the best out of your game." Early access remains "core" to the "DNA" of Unknown Worlds, as they continue with the creation of Subnautica 2, which is about to get a nourishing injection of robot frogs.

I'm writing this up mostly because I'd like to know where you all stand as regards the "very ugly, incomplete, or prototype" - which, now that I think about it, sounds like the film Sergio Leone might have made, if he'd gotten into industry documentaries rather than spaghetti westerns. My view on early access is basically that it has become the same things as live service. I'm not sure there's a meaningful division any more between labelling a game "unfinished" and the expectation that devs will keep adding stuff to any release.

Within that, though, there's a lot of diversity, as Gallegos acknowledges in the GI piece. "Early access could mean a game like ours doing long-term open development, or it could be a game three months from a 1.0 release that's effectively doing a paid beta soft launch and using the Early Access term as a way to soften player expectations," he observed.

Not everybody has been as fortunate as Unknown Worlds in persuading players to give them the benefit of the doubt. In a crowded market (GI say that 2,924 early access games have launched on Steam this year so far, citing SteamDB), newer teams may suffer from being compared to older operators like Unknown Worlds, who got involved when early access was still fresh and exotic.

Elsewhere in the GI article, Denis Dyack, CEO of Deadhaus Sonata developer Apocalypse Studios, argues that expectations are unavoidably set by the early access devs with the largest budgets, citing Subnautica 2 as an example.

Back to you, the atrocious buyer of unfinshed games: what do you expect from an early access release? What degree of wobble will you overlook? What are you happy for devs to leave out till the final version? How important is communication, really? Does it just depend totally on the game? Here is some topical music to think along to.
